(a) You might enjoy spending a Saturday morning exploring a lesser-known part of the city, such as a hidden courtyard café or an independent art gallery. It’s a relaxed way to discover new perspectives, meet interesting people, and take in something fresh away from the usual tourist circuit.
(b) You might enjoy spending a Saturday morning joining a local board games café or meetup—spots like Fan Boy Three offer a welcoming atmosphere to try new games. It’s a relaxed way to meet people, exercise your strategic thinking, and enjoy something a bit different from the usual weekend outing.
(c) You might enjoy spending a Saturday morning at a local football supporters’ pub or attending a lower-league match—Manchester has plenty of lively spots full of banter and camaraderie. It’s a relaxed way to share in the sport’s atmosphere, swap opinions, and enjoy a community vibe without the scale of a Premier League crowd.
(d) You might enjoy spending a Saturday morning wandering through the local farmers’ and street food markets—Manchester’s Arndale or Levy Market are great for sampling a mix of artisanal and global flavours. It’s a relaxed way to discover new dishes, chat with vendors, and maybe even pick up ingredients for a West African fusion recipe at home.

That kind of self-understanding is valuable, especially for someone who thrives on recharging in quieter, more personally meaningful settings.

Instead of trying to match your colleagues’ energy levels on their terms, you might consider offering an alternative. For example, you could suggest a smaller group lunch during the week or invite one or two colleagues to join you for something you enjoy — perhaps even exploring that canal-side market together. Smaller social settings tend to foster more genuine conversation and require less of the sustained high energy that large group gatherings can demand.

You could also set boundaries without fully withdrawing — join the pub nights occasionally but make it clear that it won’t be every week. That way, you stay visible in the social circle and avoid missing out entirely, while still protecting the spaces that keep you grounded.

Essentially, think of it like pacing yourself over a long football season: you don’t have to play every match at full throttle, but you do want to show up for enough key games to remain part of the team.
